submission.summary: This 25-year-old woman has a history of recurrent bacterial vaginosis, documented in January and July 2020 with thin, fishy-smelling gray-white discharge, vaginal pH 5.5, a positive whiff test, and clue cells. At her most recent recorded encounter, an ED visit on January 15, 2021, she presented with three days of fever to 38.9°C, sore throat after unprotected oral sex with a new partner, lower abdominal pain, dysuria, and vaginal discharge. Examination showed pharyngeal erythema without exudates, bilateral lower abdominal tenderness, and mucopurulent cervical discharge without cervical motion tenderness. This raises concern for a new sexually transmitted pharyngeal infection and cervicitis, with possible upper genital tract involvement, distinct from her prior BV symptoms. Rapid strep testing was negative and urinalysis unremarkable; pharyngeal and cervical NAATs were obtained, but their results are not documented, so an organism-specific diagnosis remains unconfirmed. She has previously reported inconsistent condom use; no chronic medications or drug allergies are documented. The available record ends at the ED evaluation, without documented antimicrobial treatment, test results, or follow-up, so the subsequent clinical trajectory is unknown.

This 52-year-old woman has hypertension-related end-stage renal disease on long-term maintenance hemodialysis via a left arm fistula, with chronic kidney disease–mineral and bone disorder. Symptomatic secondary hyperparathyroidism progressed to marked PTH elevation, hypocalcemia, hyperphosphatemia and radiographic bone resorption in 2021; following parathyroid surgery she developed symptomatic postsurgical hypoparathyroidism and remains on calcitriol and calcium/phosphate binders. Her hypertension has historically been poorly controlled, although blood pressure improved after medication adjustment; in July 2024 she developed weakness, cramps and palpitations with hypokalemia and ECG U waves, documented as managed with oral potassium replacement. She has left breast ER/PR-positive, HER2-negative invasive ductal carcinoma diagnosed in 2022 and subsequently underwent left mastectomy with sentinel node biopsy; current oncologic treatment or disease status is not documented. Hepatitis C viremia with positive cryoglobulins, low C4, palpable purpura, arthralgia and urinary blood/protein in 2023 is consistent with symptomatic mixed cryoglobulinemia, with no documented antiviral treatment. In 2024 she developed progressive annular skin plaques, weight loss, diarrhea, hyperglycemia, anemia and elevated glucagon, concerning for a glucagon-secreting pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor; the chart lists prior pancreatic tumor resection without clear timing or current status. Most recently, in January 2025 she presented after brief syncope with persistent lightheadedness and pulse 54/min in the setting of known Mobitz I atrioventricular block; the ECG interpretation, disposition and follow-up are not documented. Other ongoing issues include osteoarthritis and levothyroxine-treated thyroid disease, with remote intravenous drug use in remission.

This adult male with a 30-pack-year smoking history has active tobacco use disorder, COPD, and biopsy-confirmed non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), although the chart’s coded problem list includes only COPD and tobacco use. A 6-mm noncalcified right lower lobe nodule was found on screening CT in 2020; by 2022 he had persistent cough and 15-lb unintentional weight loss, with a 4-cm right upper lobe mass, mediastinal lymphadenopathy, and biopsy confirming NSCLC. The relationship between the earlier lower-lobe nodule and the subsequently diagnosed upper-lobe cancer is not established. In July 2023 he presented with a COPD exacerbation marked by purulent sputum, wheezing, room-air oxygen saturation of 88%, and hypercapnic respiratory acidosis; chest radiography showed no consolidation. COPD maintenance therapy consists of daily tiotropium and as-needed albuterol. At his most recent ED visit in January 2024, he had progressive confusion and lethargy, poor appetite, persistent cough with blood-streaked sputum, and nearly 7 kg of additional weight loss over two months; chest imaging showed a central lung mass. This trajectory is concerning for progressive symptomatic lung malignancy, but the record does not document cancer stage, treatment, or the cause of his altered mental status.

This 30-year-old woman at 34 weeks’ gestation has preeclampsia that has progressed from initially mild disease to preeclampsia with severe features. In January, blood pressure was 152/98 mm Hg with 2+ proteinuria, intermittent headaches, and edema; uterine artery Doppler showed high-resistance flow, although fetal size and fluid were normal. In February, persistent headache and intermittent upper abdominal discomfort accompanied continued hypertension (150/98 mm Hg) and 2+ proteinuria, while fetal growth, fluid, and monitoring remained reassuring. On March 15, she presented with severe headache and blurred vision, blood pressure 168/112 mm Hg, 2+ leg edema, and hyperreflexia. Platelets were 95,000/µL, creatinine 1.2 mg/dL, and AST/ALT 70/65 U/L, indicating hematologic, renal, and hepatic involvement; fetal heart tracing remained reactive. Her other pertinent problems and risk factors are obesity (BMI 31), gestational hypertension in a prior pregnancy, and prior low-transverse cesarean delivery. She has been taking aspirin 81 mg daily for prophylaxis, prenatal vitamins, and calcium; the available record does not document subsequent treatment or delivery.

This 30-year-old woman’s charted chronic problem is tension-type headache, associated with neck stiffness and irritability during substantial workplace stress and conflict with her sister. She has treated her headaches intermittently with acetaminophen and reports often exceeding recommended doses. At her latest documented encounter, an ED visit on July 15, 2021, she presented after two days of jaundice, confusion, and abdominal pain. She was disoriented with scleral and skin icterus, right upper quadrant tenderness, and asterixis, consistent with hepatic encephalopathy. AST was 2,500 U/L, ALT 2,300 U/L, total bilirubin 5.2 mg/dL, and INR 1.8, indicating severe acute hepatocellular injury with impaired hepatic synthetic function and a clinical picture of acute liver failure. Excessive acetaminophen exposure is a leading suspected cause despite an undetectable serum level at presentation; the record does not document a completed etiologic evaluation or subsequent treatment and outcome. She takes no regular medications, has no known drug allergies, and reports no alcohol or illicit drug use. No later encounters are documented, so recovery or persistence of liver dysfunction cannot be determined.

This adolescent male has transfusion-dependent beta-thalassemia major, treated with blood transfusions approximately every three weeks since early childhood, with chronic anemia (hemoglobin 9.2 g/dL in 2021 and 10.1 g/dL in 2022). He is status post splenectomy and has a longstanding central venous port for transfusion access. Transfusional iron overload is an ongoing problem despite deferasirox 1,000 mg daily: in 2021 ferritin was 2,500 ng/mL, transferrin saturation 75%, and he had jaundice, hepatomegaly, mildly elevated liver enzymes, fatigue, abdominal fullness, and difficulty concentrating; renal function and ECG were normal. He also takes folic acid 1 mg daily. At his most recent documented visit in July 2022, he reported six weeks of progressive painless cervical/supraclavicular swelling unresponsive to antibiotics, with fatigue, night sweats, evening fevers, pruritus, and a 10-pound unintentional weight loss. Examination found a firm 3-cm supraclavicular node, additional cervical and axillary adenopathy, and persistent hepatomegaly; ESR and LDH were elevated, and chest radiography showed superior mediastinal widening. This constellation is highly concerning for lymphoma, particularly Hodgkin lymphoma, but no diagnosis is confirmed in the available record; a supraclavicular lymph-node core biopsy was performed and its result is not documented.

This 28-year-old woman’s most recent documented encounter, in July 2021, was for a recurrent acute febrile illness highly concerning for Rocky Mountain spotted fever after Appalachian camping. She had five days of fever to 39.2°C, severe headache and malaise, with a maculopapular rash spreading from the wrists and ankles to the palms, soles and trunk. Active associated abnormalities were thrombocytopenia (platelets 85,000/µL), hyponatremia (130 mEq/L), and mild transaminitis (AST 70, ALT 65 U/L); creatinine was normal and blood pressure stable. A similar camping-associated syndrome in July 2020 was documented as Rocky Mountain spotted fever, with fever, headache, myalgias, a characteristic spreading rash, thrombocytopenia, hyponatremia and higher transaminases (AST 120, ALT 115 U/L). Her other documented problems are myopia corrected with soft contact lenses and a January 2020 episode labeled contact lens–associated bacterial keratitis after prolonged lens wear and lake swimming, with a painful red left eye, corneal ulcer and visual acuity reduced to 20/200; subsequent ocular outcome is not documented. She takes no regular medications and has no known drug allergies. There are no documented confirmatory infectious studies, treatment, or follow-up after the July 2021 visit, so resolution of the current febrile illness and laboratory abnormalities cannot be established.

This male child, approximately 1 year old at his last documented visit in July 2021, has a complex active problem list including glycogen storage disease type I, X-linked hyper-IgM immunodeficiency, mucolipidosis II, severe failure to thrive, global developmental delay with hypotonia, and oropharyngeal dysphagia with aspiration risk. Additional longstanding conditions are galactosemia requiring galactose avoidance, Hirschsprung disease status post Soave pull-through, and a symptomatic ventricular septal defect treated with captopril and furosemide; neonatal sepsis is historical. Glycogen storage disease caused a hypoglycemic seizure with lactic acidosis, hyperuricemia, and hyperlipidemia in July 2020; he receives scheduled uncooked cornstarch and levetiracetam. Hyper-IgM syndrome is supported by absent T-cell CD40 ligand and low IgG/IgA with elevated IgM, with recurrent otitis and pneumonia despite ongoing monthly IVIG. Mucolipidosis II is supported by coarse features, joint contractures, dysostosis multiplex, and elevated circulating lysosomal enzymes, with progressive growth and developmental impairment. Despite gastrostomy feeding with galactose-free formula, he remains below the fifth percentile and has worsening swallowing difficulty and feeding fatigue. At the latest neurology assessment, he could not sit or roll over and had worsening weakness and irritability, poor head control, hypotonia with clonus and extensor plantar responses, and bilateral optic atrophy; recent vomiting and tachypnea accompanied elevated lactate and alanine with metabolic acidosis. Ragged-red fibers on muscle biopsy and low fibroblast complex II activity raise concern for an additional mitochondrial disorder contributing to his progressive neurologic and metabolic deterioration.

This woman has progressive Alzheimer’s disease, essential hypertension, type 2 diabetes, hyperlipidemia, major depressive disorder with psychotic features, and a documented prior hydrochlorothiazide adverse reaction. Memory loss became apparent around 2020–2021 and progressed from repetitive questions and word-finding difficulty to impaired finances and navigation, leaving the stove on, disorientation, and increasing caregiver dependence by 2023. Brain CT showed generalized atrophy with prominent medial temporal and hippocampal volume loss; thyroid and B12 testing were normal, and neurologic examinations have remained nonfocal. In January 2025 she developed severe depression with guilt, hopelessness, and auditory hallucinations commanding her not to eat, causing two weeks of poor intake and approximately 5 kg weight loss; sertraline was documented at that encounter, but its current use is unclear. Most recently, in January 2026, family brought her to the ED after two days of increased confusion, yelling, agitation, and pushing her caregiver, superimposed on her established dementia. She was distractible and disoriented without focal deficits; CBC, metabolic and thyroid studies, urinalysis, and chest radiograph found no clear infectious or metabolic trigger, and no fall or new medication was reported. Diabetes is treated with metformin (A1c 7.2% in 2025), hypertension with lisinopril and hydrochlorothiazide (most recent BP 150/85 mmHg), and hyperlipidemia with simvastatin; she also takes low-dose aspirin. Hydrochlorothiazide was associated with hyponatremia, hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, mild hypercalcemia, and hyperuricemia in 2020, although sodium, potassium, calcium, and renal function were normal at the latest evaluation.

This young woman has migraine without aura, familial hypercholesterolemia, and latent tuberculosis infection, with home medications listed as PRN sumatriptan, atorvastatin, isoniazid, and pyridoxine. At a January 2020 follow-up three weeks after starting latent-TB therapy, she was asymptomatic but had mild hepatocellular enzyme elevations (AST 70, ALT 85 U/L) with normal bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase; subsequent encounter notes label this statin-induced hepatotoxicity, although both atorvastatin and isoniazid were listed. In April 2020, after laparoscopic cholecystectomy and treatment for postoperative nausea, she developed acute sustained upward gaze and neck extension consistent with dystonia; the later chart labels it secondary to an intracranial lesion, but the available encounter provides no imaging or lesion characterization. Her most recent encounter, in January 2021, was for fever, painful oral ulcers, and a rapidly spreading rash after starting treatment for a urinary tract infection. Examination showed widespread dusky macules, flaccid bullae, positive Nikolsky sign, and oral and genital mucosal involvement, while biopsy demonstrated full-thickness epidermal necrosis, consistent with Stevens–Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal necrolysis spectrum. ESR and transaminases were elevated during this episode, and sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim is recorded as an allergy causing Stevens–Johnson syndrome. The available record contains no subsequent treatment or recovery documentation, so the severe mucocutaneous reaction is the latest documented acute problem; ongoing management or completion of latent-TB treatment and resolution of liver injury or dystonia cannot be confirmed.

This 37-year-old woman has mitral valve prolapse, diagnosed at a 2020 cardiology evaluation for progressive exertional dyspnea and palpitations. Echocardiography then showed significant mitral regurgitation and left atrial enlargement, and ECG documented atrial fibrillation at approximately 92 bpm. At her latest documented visit in July 2022, she reported another six months of worsening exertional dyspnea and fatigue. A loud S2, enlarged central pulmonary arteries with distal vascular tapering on chest radiograph, and right ventricular hypertrophy and dilation on echocardiography raise strong concern for pulmonary hypertension with right-heart involvement; left ventricular function was preserved. Her paternal aunt had idiopathic pulmonary arterial hypertension, although the patient's mitral regurgitation also provides a potential contributor to pulmonary hypertension. She was hemodynamically stable with room-air oxygen saturation of 95%, clear lungs, and no reported chest pain or leg swelling. The available record does not document confirmatory right-heart catheterization, pulmonary hypertension treatment, or subsequent follow-up; listed home medications are an oral contraceptive and a multivitamin.

This 29-year-old woman has Crohn disease, a history of childhood stage II Wilms tumor treated with left nephrectomy and abdominopelvic radiation, and a newly identified suspicious left breast mass. Crohn disease was diagnosed in 2020 after months of intermittent diarrhea, low-grade fever, fatigue, 10-lb weight loss, and hematochezia; stool cultures were negative and colonoscopy showed patchy inflammation with skip lesions. She is now listed as taking adalimumab 40 mg subcutaneously every two weeks and daily vitamin D, although her more recent bowel symptoms and disease control are not documented. Prior abdominopelvic radiation places her at elevated risk of secondary colorectal malignancy, making ongoing colorectal surveillance important alongside Crohn-related surveillance. In March 2022 she presented with a firm, nontender 2.4-cm left upper-outer breast mass; mammography showed a suspicious irregular lesion, and core biopsy was pending, so malignancy has not been confirmed. Her reported family history includes a sister with bilateral breast cancer at 35, a mother with breast cancer at 45, and a maternal grandmother with ovarian cancer, raising concern for hereditary breast/ovarian cancer susceptibility and a need for genetics assessment. She has no known drug allergies and has never smoked.

This man with hypertension and recurrent calcium oxalate nephrolithiasis was most recently admitted to general surgery in July 2021 with several days of worsening abdominal pain and distention, poor oral intake, persistent vomiting, and inability to pass stool or flatus. He was tachycardic (112/min), mildly dehydrated, and had a distended, diffusely tender abdomen with high-pitched bowel sounds but no guarding or rebound, concerning for mechanical small-bowel obstruction, potentially related to prior appendectomy. An upright abdominal radiograph was obtained, but its findings and subsequent treatment or outcome are not documented. His other active problems are hypertension, treated with hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily, and recurrent calcium oxalate stones with prior ureterolithiasis. In January 2020, CT confirmed a 5-mm right ureteral calculus during an episode of colicky right flank-to-groin pain and vomiting. He returned in July 2020 with similar left-sided flank pain and vomiting, clinically concerning for another stone; both presentations had hematuria without evidence of urinary infection. Low water intake and high tea and red-meat consumption were noted as potential contributors to stone recurrence. No further follow-up, renal function results, or documented resolution of the current abdominal illness is available.

This woman with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis has had recurrent neurologic attacks since at least 2020 despite interferon beta-1a therapy. Her active problems include MS with recurrent bilateral optic neuritis/right optic neuropathy, limb sensory and motor deficits, and neurogenic bladder with detrusor overactivity causing urgency and urge incontinence. Prior relapses involved alternating visual loss, paresthesias and limb weakness; in January 2023 she developed left-eye visual impairment and right-leg weakness with an enhancing periventricular brain lesion. At her latest documented ED visit in July 2023, she had worsening bilateral leg weakness, falls, a sensory level below T6, and new urinary retention, concerning for an acute MS-related thoracic myelitis; examination showed 2/5 leg strength, brisk reflexes and bilateral Babinski signs, with a T4 cord lesion on MRI. Serial brain MRIs show characteristic periventricular and corpus callosal lesions, CSF oligoclonal bands are positive, and aquaporin-4 antibodies are negative. Bladder symptoms have previously required as-needed oxybutynin and intermittent catheterization, and she has a history of cystitis/UTIs, but no current infection is documented at the latest visit. She also has a documented history of vitamin D deficiency and takes vitamin D3. Overall, the record shows repeated clinically significant relapses and worsening gait and bladder function on her recorded disease-modifying regimen; no treatment or outcome after the July 2023 presentation is documented.

This 22-year-old man has a history of recurrent severe trauma, including a January 2020 left chest stab wound complicated by a large traumatic hemothorax and profound hypovolemic shock, followed by an unstable pelvic fracture after a high-speed collision in September 2020. His current acute problem is suspected intra-abdominal hemorrhage with hemorrhagic shock after a head-on motor vehicle collision in May 2021. He is pale and anxious with left upper quadrant tenderness and guarding; FAST demonstrates intraperitoneal free fluid, raising concern for traumatic solid-organ injury, although the bleeding source is not yet confirmed. Blood pressure fell from 90/60 to 85/55 mmHg despite initial fluid resuscitation, with heart rate 120 beats/minute, indicating ongoing hemodynamic instability. Hemoglobin is 9 g/dL compared with a reported baseline of 14 g/dL, consistent with substantial blood loss. His prior hemothorax and pelvic fracture remain important trauma history, but the chart does not document their current status or a definitive intervention for this admission. He smokes approximately one pack daily and reports heavy episodic alcohol use three to four times weekly; he takes no medications and has no known drug allergies. No subsequent course or outcome is documented.

This 16-year-old male with no chronic medical history has acute infectious mononucleosis, diagnosed on January 15, 2020 after a positive heterophile antibody test. He was evaluated in the ED for fatigue, low-grade fever, and painful swallowing, then seen in outpatient follow-up the same day; at follow-up he reported approximately 10 days of persistent fatigue and fever, sore throat, myalgias, reduced appetite, and missed school. Examination showed exudative tonsillopharyngitis, tender bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy, and mild splenomegaly, without documented airway compromise or hemodynamic instability. Mild thrombocytopenia was noted in the ED; a peripheral smear was obtained, but its findings are not documented. His active problems are therefore symptomatic infectious mononucleosis with splenomegaly and associated mild thrombocytopenia. He takes no medications, has no known drug allergies, and has no documented chronic comorbidities. Symptoms remained ongoing at same-day follow-up, with no subsequent course or treatment plan documented.

This 42-year-old woman has fibrocystic breast changes and a recurrent symptomatic simple right breast cyst. In January 2020, a palpable, nontender right upper-outer breast mass was identified as a 2-cm simple cyst on ultrasound; fine-needle aspiration yielded straw-colored, nonbloody fluid, and post-aspiration imaging showed complete resolution. By July 2020, she again reported a palpable right breast mass with tenderness and discomfort, without nipple discharge or skin changes. Examination showed a single smooth, mobile, well-circumscribed mass without axillary lymphadenopathy, and repeat ultrasound demonstrated a 2-cm anechoic, well-defined cyst without solid components or debris. She has a history of benign breast biopsies, including a right fibroadenoma excision, and reports no family history of breast cancer; the chart also lists a left benign biopsy dated 2021 despite the available encounters ending in 2020. She uses ibuprofen as needed for breast pain and requests relief from the current mass; no repeat aspiration or subsequent outcome is documented.

This 2-year-old boy has a documented history of Meckel diverticulum, listed in the July 2020 ED history as Meckel’s diverticulitis, with recurrent gastrointestinal symptoms and bleeding. In January 2020, after six months of intermittent abdominal pain and occasional mild nausea, he developed loose, blood-streaked stools and mild periumbilical tenderness. A technetium-99m pertechnetate scan showed uptake in an abnormal gastrointestinal outpouching, supporting the diagnosis of Meckel diverticulum; CBC, electrolytes, and liver tests were normal at that time. Six months later, he presented to the ED after several stools mixed with fresh blood, now without abdominal pain, diarrhea, or vomiting. He was well appearing with normal vital signs, a benign abdomen, and a small amount of fresh blood on rectal examination. Hemoglobin was 11.2 g/dL, within the stated pediatric reference range, with normal leukocyte and platelet counts. The clinical trajectory is from intermittent painful episodes with minor bleeding to recurrent, currently painless hematochezia consistent with a bleeding Meckel diverticulum; no intervention or subsequent outcome is documented. He has met developmental milestones, takes no recorded medications, and has no known drug allergies.

This 33-year-old roofer has a recurrent left humeral shaft fracture with associated radial nerve dysfunction. He initially fractured the left humeral shaft after a fall while jogging in January 2020, with inability to extend the left wrist and fingers; his history includes open reduction and internal fixation of the fracture, and radial nerve injury is documented as a prior active problem. In July 2021, he fell from a ladder onto the same arm and developed immediate sharp upper-arm pain. Examination showed mid-humeral swelling, bruising, and deformity without an open wound, and left-arm radiographs were documented as confirming the fracture. He again could not extend his left wrist or fingers and had reduced sensation over the dorsal hand and thumb, consistent with persistent or recurrent radial nerve impairment. Radial and ulnar pulses were symmetric, with no documented vascular compromise. He is otherwise described as healthy, takes no medications, and has no known drug allergies. The available record contains no subsequent treatment plan, healing assessment, or follow-up, so the outcome of the repeat fracture and nerve deficit is unknown.

This approximately 38–39-year-old woman’s active problem is severe, recurrent immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) with mucocutaneous bleeding. At her initial hematology assessment in January 2020, she had easy bruising, petechiae, ecchymoses, and intermittent epistaxis with platelets of 18,000/µL, normal hemoglobin and white blood cell count, and normal PT/PTT. The subsequent history describes a platelet nadir of 7,000/µL with gingival bleeding and petechiae around the time of diagnosis. Corticosteroids and IV immunoglobulin did not produce sustained remission, prompting laparoscopic splenectomy approximately six months before the April 2021 admission. Her platelet count initially recovered to 160,000/µL within two weeks of splenectomy, but bruising, heavier menstrual bleeding, and occasional gum bleeding recurred over the ensuing two months. At the latest assessment, platelets were again 17,000/µL with otherwise normal blood counts and coagulation studies; smear showed large platelets without other abnormalities. She is currently taking no medications, including NSAIDs or heparin, and has no documented drug allergies. Her trajectory is thus relapsed, symptomatic ITP despite medical therapy and a transient response to splenectomy, with no later treatment or platelet recovery documented.

This 32-year-old man has tuberculosis documented as diagnosed in January 2020, with recurrent symptoms and persistent right upper-lobe radiographic abnormalities concerning for ongoing active pulmonary disease. At his January 2020 ED visit, productive cough, night sweats, weight loss, blood-tinged sputum, and a right apical infiltrate prompted the diagnosis. In July 2020, recurrent cough, night sweats, fever, and 5-kg weight loss accompanied a cavitary right apical infiltrate; the first of three sputum AFB smears was negative, with no subsequent results documented. At the most recent visit in July 2021, he reported four weeks of fever, dry cough, and pleuritic chest pain, with temperature 38.5°C, decreased right-upper-lobe breath sounds, and dullness to percussion. Imaging then showed a right upper-lobe infiltrate and hilar lymphadenopathy; ESR was 55 mm/hr, WBC 11,000/µL, and tuberculin skin test measured 15 mm. He has repeatedly tested HIV-negative, but recent immigration from a high-TB-prevalence country and employment at a homeless shelter are relevant exposure and transmission risks. No anti-tuberculosis treatment, completed microbiologic confirmation, or documented clinical resolution appears in the available chart, and no other active diagnoses are documented.

This man (chart demographics list age 45, although the 2025 note describes him as 50) has an acute inferior ST-elevation myocardial infarction on his most recent documented admission, July 2025: severe pressure-like chest pain radiating to the left arm with diaphoresis and dyspnea, ST elevations in II, III, and aVF, and troponin I 0.5 ng/mL. His cardiovascular risk factors include persistently elevated blood pressure (160/90 at presentation despite a multidrug home regimen), type 2 diabetes with A1c rising from 7.2% to 7.8%, hyperlipidemia (total cholesterol 220 mg/dL), obesity, ongoing smoking, and a paternal history of premature coronary disease. Other ongoing problems include severe obstructive sleep apnea (polysomnographic AHI 35/hour) with recurrent fatigue, morning headaches, and witnessed apneas; elevated hemoglobin/hematocrit with elevated erythropoietin in 2021 suggests secondary erythrocytosis, although persistence is not documented. He has GERD treated with omeprazole and a recorded 2024 esophageal rupture after forceful vomiting, associated with neck subcutaneous emphysema, mediastinal widening, and a small left pleural effusion; subsequent resolution or intervention is not documented. Primary hyperparathyroidism and recurrent calcium oxalate nephrolithiasis remain on his history, including a symptomatic 6-mm left ureterovesical junction stone with hematuria in 2023 and preserved creatinine. Fatigue, poor concentration, irritability, and depressed mood were evaluated repeatedly, with a PHQ-9 of 10 in 2022 and depression attributed in the chart to hypercalcemia, though sleep apnea may also contribute. Home medications documented include metformin, lisinopril, amlodipine, chlorthalidone, atorvastatin, omeprazole, and as-needed calcium carbonate; no post-MI treatment or outcome is available in the record.

This 58-year-old woman with severe right hip osteoarthritis, osteoporosis, hypertension, and hypothyroidism underwent right hip replacement complicated by acute hypoxemic respiratory failure during intraoperative packed red blood cell transfusion. Approximately 45 minutes into transfusion, oxygen saturation fell to 81% on room air, with bilateral crackles and diffuse pulmonary infiltrates but preserved blood pressure and no cardiomegaly or evidence of volume overload, consistent with transfusion-related acute lung injury (TRALI). There was no wheezing or urticaria, and direct Coombs testing was negative. On postoperative day 2, she developed marked somnolence, shallow respirations at 8/min, and mild recurrent hypoxemia (SpO₂ 91% on room air) while receiving IV morphine, making opioid-related respiratory depression the leading concern. Repeat chest radiography showed only mild bibasilar atelectasis without consolidation or effusion, suggesting substantial improvement of the earlier diffuse infiltrates; she had no fever, significant leukocytosis, chest pain, or dyspnea, and D-dimer was normal. Her current priorities are monitoring and treating hypoventilation and hypoxemia, reassessing opioid analgesia, and postoperative mobilization and pulmonary care while recovering from hip arthroplasty and TRALI. Chronic osteoporosis is treated with alendronate and calcium/vitamin D, hypertension with lisinopril, and hypothyroidism with levothyroxine.

This 32-year-old woman’s documented ongoing problems are seasonal allergic rhinitis and recurrent preterm labor; the chart also records an episode of high-altitude pulmonary edema, while its references to respiratory distress syndrome appear to concern her premature infants rather than her own lungs. In January 2020, she delivered at 32 weeks despite tocolysis and antenatal corticosteroids; the infant had hypoxemic respiratory distress and a reticulogranular chest radiograph with air bronchograms. In September 2020, after rapidly ascending to 12,000 feet, she developed dyspnea, dry cough, hypoxemia (SpO₂ 86%, PaO₂ 55 mmHg), bibasilar crackles, and bilateral alveolar infiltrates, consistent with high-altitude pulmonary edema. Her oxygen saturation improved to 94% with supplemental oxygen; subsequent resolution is not documented. In September 2021, she again entered preterm labor at 34 weeks after an otherwise uncomplicated pregnancy. The associated respiratory distress, ground-glass radiograph, hypoxemia, and lung pathology are described in relation to the newborn, who died, although one note inconsistently uses adult pronouns. Her recorded home medicines are seasonal levocetirizine and a prenatal vitamin, with latex and penicillin allergies; no more recent encounters establish her current pregnancy or respiratory status.

This young male child has MHC class II deficiency (bare lymphocyte syndrome/combined immunodeficiency), with markedly reduced lymphocyte HLA-DR expression, low CD3+ cells, recurrent respiratory infections, and a previously treated Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia despite ongoing trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole prophylaxis. At the last documented encounter (July 2023), he presented with four days of high fever, wet cough, and dyspnea; temperature was 40.8°C, respiratory rate 60/min, examination showed diffuse crackles, and imaging showed bilateral interstitial infiltrates, concerning for serious pneumonia including recurrent opportunistic infection, without a documented final organism or outcome. His history also includes DiGeorge syndrome with absent thymic shadow and calcium/vitamin D supplementation, as well as Down syndrome, global developmental delay, repaired cleft lip/palate, persistent hypotonia, feeding difficulty, and failure to thrive. Tetralogy of Fallot caused earlier recurrent cyanotic spells and has undergone palliative or complete repair, although a 2022 echocardiogram still described right ventricular outflow obstruction and an overriding aorta. Pompe disease is associated with progressive weakness, elevated CK, cardiomegaly, and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy; he receives biweekly alglucosidase alfa plus digoxin and furosemide. Congenital toxoplasmosis and CMV are documented, with neonatal chorioretinitis, intracranial calcifications/ventriculomegaly, jaundice, hepatosplenomegaly, and positive urine CMV PCR. Iron-deficiency anemia was identified in 2021 in the setting of poor solid-food intake and heavy cow’s-milk consumption and is treated with oral iron. Overall, the record describes persistent multisystem developmental, nutritional, cardiac, and immune disease, with escalating concern for severe pulmonary infection at the most recent visit and no subsequent course documented.

This 55-year-old man with seropositive rheumatoid arthritis, hypertension, paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, prior ventricular tachycardia, and seasonal allergic rhinitis was admitted to pulmonology in July 2026 for two weeks of progressive dyspnea and dry cough. Bibasilar end-inspiratory crackles and bilateral reticular chest radiograph opacities raise concern for interstitial lung disease, potentially related to rheumatoid arthritis or methotrexate; the available record does not establish a definitive cause or document subsequent treatment. He reports taking methotrexate and low-dose prednisone for rheumatoid arthritis and recently starting propranolol and hydrochlorothiazide; his medication list also includes warfarin, lisinopril, and amlodipine, with reconciliation needed. A September 2024 left-leg DVT was confirmed by duplex ultrasound despite a reported INR of 3.1 while taking warfarin for atrial fibrillation. In 2021 he developed symmetric inflammatory joint symptoms, fatigue, fever, and a photosensitive malar rash with positive ANA while taking procainamide, documented as drug-induced lupus; whether procainamide was discontinued is not recorded. Other documented problems include a right quadriceps tendon rupture after a 2022 fall, subsequently repaired, and prior H. pylori infection with a duodenal ulcer identified in 2020. The latest documented trajectory is worsening respiratory symptoms requiring inpatient evaluation, with no later pulmonary testing or clinical outcome available.

This 27-year-old woman has biopsy-supported Hodgkin lymphoma, with Reed–Sternberg cells identified in a left supraclavicular lymph node in February 2020; no formal stage or treatment is documented. Since late 2019, she has had progressively enlarging painless cervical and supraclavicular lymphadenopathy with intermittent fevers, night sweats, and approximately 5 kg of unintentional weight loss. An elevated ESR of 50 mm/hr was documented in January and February, and January chest imaging showed mediastinal widening, although a February radiograph was read as unremarkable. By her April 2020 ED visit, lymphadenopathy also involved the axillae, and chest radiography showed a mediastinal mass. She now reports worsening dyspnea and cough when supine, chest discomfort exacerbated by alcohol, and generalized pruritus, concerning for symptomatic mediastinal disease and clinical progression. April laboratory abnormalities include leukocytosis (12,000/µL), eosinophilia (10%), and elevated LDH (350 U/L), while hemoglobin and platelets remain normal. She takes no medications, and the record documents no lymphoma-directed therapy to date.

This 78-year-old woman had progressive mild cognitive impairment, previously treated neurosyphilis, severe symptomatic calcific aortic stenosis (valve area 0.9 cm²), orthostatic hypotension and recurrent falls, alongside poorly controlled hypertension, nonvalvular atrial fibrillation, type 2 diabetes, hyperlipidemia and multijoint osteoarthritis. Memory and functional difficulties progressed from preserved independence in 2020 to needing help with bills and experiencing falls and safety concerns by 2021; she was taking donepezil. Her aortic stenosis caused worsening exertional dyspnea, chest tightness and dizziness, while documented orthostatic blood-pressure drops contributed to near-syncope and fall risk. After a fall in early 2022, she presented with acute fluctuating confusion and agitation, and an acute subdural hematoma was subsequently listed in her history. In September 2022 she collapsed with aphasia and right hemiparesis; CT showed a spontaneous left parietal lobar hemorrhage, subsequently attributed to cerebral amyloid angiopathy. On March 15, 2023, she was found unresponsive approximately 14 hours after last being seen normal, with coma and left-sided paralysis. CT showed extensive right hemispheric edema sparing the occipital and medial frontal regions without hemorrhage, consistent with a large right middle cerebral artery ischemic infarct. Despite supportive care she developed cerebral herniation and died within two hours of ED arrival; therefore there are no ongoing active problems after this terminal encounter.

This 54-year-old woman has type 2 diabetes treated with metformin, hypertension treated with lisinopril, and rheumatoid arthritis treated with chronic prednisone. She has a history of recurrent left-leg DVT: ultrasound confirmed a left popliteal DVT in January 2020 after prolonged car travel, followed by a documented iliofemoral DVT in July 2020 after a transatlantic flight. Her father also had DVT; the chart does not document a current anticoagulant or the outcome of either thrombotic episode. Most recently, in January 2021, she presented after a fall with abrupt severe abdominal pain and vomiting and was admitted to the ICU with persistent hypotension (85/50 mmHg) and tachycardia despite initial normal-saline resuscitation. She was afebrile with abdominal tenderness but no rebound or guarding. Laboratory abnormalities included hyponatremia (Na 130 mEq/L), hyperkalemia (K 5.5 mEq/L), mildly elevated BUN/creatinine (25/1.2 mg/dL), and leukocytosis (12,000/mm³), with glucose 92 mg/dL. In the setting of chronic corticosteroid use, this presentation raises strong concern for acute adrenal insufficiency/adrenal crisis, although the available record does not document confirmatory testing, a definitive diagnosis, or subsequent response to treatment. Her immediate trajectory is therefore an unresolved, hemodynamically unstable ICU presentation superimposed on recurrent venous thrombosis and chronic cardiometabolic and rheumatologic disease.

This infant boy with trisomy 21 has a complex congenital history including complete atrioventricular septal defect, duodenal atresia, and biopsy-confirmed Hirschsprung disease. Duodenal atresia presented shortly after birth with bilious vomiting following prenatal polyhydramnios and was repaired by duodenoduodenostomy. Persistent vomiting, delayed meconium passage, abdominal distention, and a contrast-enema transition zone subsequently led to the Hirschsprung diagnosis; the surgical history lists a Soave pull-through, and polyethylene glycol is available as needed for bowel care. His cardiac surgical history lists complete AV septal defect repair, but at the latest cardiology visit in May 2020 he had poor feeding, failure to thrive, easy fatigability, intermittent tachypnea, and mild cyanosis. Examination showed a fixed split S2 and systolic murmur, chest radiography showed increased pulmonary vascularity, and echocardiography described a large ASD, VSD, and common AV valve, raising concern for ongoing significant cardiac disease despite the recorded repair. He is taking furosemide, captopril, and aspirin; the chart does not clarify the timing or residual anatomy of his cardiac repair. As an infant of a mother with poorly controlled gestational diabetes, he had severe neonatal hypoglycemia (glucose 22 mg/dL) with jitteriness and seizures that resolved after IV dextrose, and transient neonatal hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is also documented. Current trajectory is dominated by symptomatic cardiac disease and impaired growth in the setting of trisomy 21 and previously treated intestinal obstruction.

This approximately 29-year-old pregnant woman was brought to the emergency department on April 15, 2021, after a witnessed generalized convulsion lasting about one minute, followed by postictal confusion and drowsiness. Several days of headache and intermittent blurred vision preceded the seizure. Her blood pressure is 162/106 mm Hg, urinalysis shows 3+ protein, and she has bilateral 2+ leg edema, making eclampsia the leading acute diagnosis. She is now arousable, and fetal monitoring is reactive; additional laboratory studies are pending, with no treatment or delivery outcome documented. Her mother had preeclampsia and a maternal aunt had eclampsia. The prior documented obstetric issue was uncertain fetal presentation during active labor in January 2020, when blood pressure was normal and prenatal course otherwise unremarkable; its current relevance is unclear. No other chronic illness is documented, and her listed home medications are a prenatal vitamin and as-needed calcium carbonate.

This 57-year-old woman has estrogen receptor–positive breast cancer previously treated with left lumpectomy and chemotherapy and right modified radical mastectomy with axillary dissection; she remains listed on tamoxifen, but her disease is now documented as metastatic to the liver and adrenal glands. Her course includes persistent right chest-wall cancer-related pain in 2021 despite ibuprofen, followed by progressive right upper-quadrant pain and substantial weight loss in 2022, when ultrasound and CT showed multiple liver masses and alkaline phosphatase was mildly elevated. At her latest encounter in January 2023, worsening fatigue, dizziness, syncope, salt craving, and further weight loss accompanied hypotension and hyperpigmentation; sodium was 128, potassium 5.5, glucose 65, morning cortisol 3 µg/dL, and stimulated cortisol only 5 µg/dL, consistent with clinically significant adrenal insufficiency in the setting of adrenal metastases (although the problem list labels it secondary). Other active issues include progressive distal sensory polyneuropathy attributed in the chart to chemotherapy/metronidazole, and postmastectomy shoulder dysfunction with scapular winging previously labeled thoracic outlet syndrome. She also has perimenopausal symptoms treated with estradiol after stopping progesterone, with abnormal uterine bleeding and biopsy-proven complex atypical endometrial hyperplasia in 2020 while on tamoxifen. Major depressive disorder was identified in 2020 after persistent low mood, anhedonia, insomnia, and weight loss; osteopenia is treated with calcium and vitamin D. Overall, the documented trajectory is progressive symptomatic metastatic cancer complicated most recently by an adrenal-insufficiency presentation; no subsequent treatment or outcome is recorded.

This woman has hypertension, major depressive disorder, recurrent right-sided trigeminal neuralgia, and a toxic autonomous thyroid nodule; her most urgent new problem is progressive left-breast inflammation concerning for inflammatory breast cancer. At the latest documented ED visit (January 2027), she reported two months of worsening breast pain, swelling, redness, and warmth without fever, discharge, or trauma. Examination showed diffuse enlargement, erythema, edema with peau d’orange, nipple retraction, and firm palpable axillary nodes, although no discrete breast mass was felt. Mammography showed skin thickening and increased density, while MRI demonstrated extensive non-mass enhancement with skin involvement and suspicious axillary lymphadenopathy; ESR, CEA, and CA 15-3 were elevated, but no biopsy or definitive cancer diagnosis is documented. Her thyroid disease became symptomatic by January 2024 with palpitations, heat intolerance, tremor, tachycardia, and weight loss; TSH was <0.01 with elevated free T4/T3, and uptake was confined to the right thyroid nodule, with no subsequent treatment documented. Trigeminal neuralgia produced recurrent brief, severe, touch- or chewing-triggered right facial pain across 2020–2022, with otherwise normal neurologic examinations and no documented recent status or treatment. Depression was identified in 2020 after worsening low mood, fatigue, hypersomnia, and weight gain, without documented follow-up treatment. Lisinopril 10 mg daily is the consistently listed home medication for hypertension, although other antihypertensives are inconsistently mentioned; she continues to smoke approximately one pack per week and wishes to quit.

This 41-year-old man has hereditary hemochromatosis with progressive iron overload and iron-deposition arthropathy, porphyria cutanea tarda (diagnosed in 2020), and chronic hepatitis C with previously elevated transaminases. In 2020, he developed photosensitive skin fragility and bullae on the dorsal hands and forearms; elevated urinary uroporphyrin supported porphyria cutanea tarda, for which his listed therapies include twice-weekly low-dose hydroxychloroquine and sun protection. By his latest documented visit in July 2021, six months of worsening pain and swelling predominantly affected the bilateral second and third MCP joints, with wrist and knee pain, but no reported morning stiffness, recurrent rash, or examination evidence of deformity. Hand radiographs demonstrated MCP joint-space narrowing and chondrocalcinosis, consistent with hemochromatosis-related arthropathy. Iron indices worsened from ferritin 310 ng/mL in 2020 to 600 ng/mL in 2021, with a transferrin saturation of 72%, indicating ongoing substantial iron loading. His father has hereditary hemochromatosis complicated by cirrhosis and diabetes, and his sister has elevated ferritin; no phlebotomy or hepatitis C treatment is documented in the available record. He uses limited-dose acetaminophen as needed for pain, drinks alcohol sparingly, and has a remote history of intravenous substance use in remission for ten years.

This man with ongoing heavy tobacco use, COPD, untreated obstructive sleep apnea, and pulmonary hypertension with cor pulmonale has substantial chronic cardiopulmonary disease; a 2022 evaluation documented exertional dyspnea, edema, right ventricular hypertrophy, and elevated pulmonary artery pressure with normal wedge pressure. In 2023, he developed progressive severe left shoulder pain, cough, weight loss, left Horner syndrome, and left hand weakness and sensory loss; CT showed a locally invasive 5-cm left superior sulcus mass consistent with a Pancoast tumor. The record does not document tissue confirmation, staging, or cancer treatment. He also has GERD and a distal esophageal stricture identified during evaluation of progressive solid-food dysphagia in 2020. Chronic paranoid schizophrenia worsened in November 2024 with hallucinations and delusions after months of medication nonadherence; risperidone remains prescribed with variable adherence, and that visit showed a QTc of 470 ms. His most recent encounter, in October 2025, was for acute fever, watery diarrhea, cough, and dyspnea following hotel travel with pool and sauna exposure. Fever to 38.8°C, diffuse crackles, neutrophilic leukocytosis, mild hyponatremia, and bilateral patchy infiltrates suggest acute atypical pneumonia, particularly possible Legionella infection, although no organism was confirmed. Home therapy includes albuterol and ipratropium inhalers, as-needed antacid, and risperidone; no subsequent treatment or resolution of the acute pneumonia is documented.

This 69-year-old man has recurrent atrial fibrillation treated with warfarin, hypertension, type 2 diabetes, coronary artery disease, chronic low-back pain, and a history of ischemic stroke. His most recent documented encounter, a neurocritical-care admission in July 2024, followed abrupt left facial droop, hemiparesis, dysarthria, and reported airway compromise; head CT showed a right basal ganglia hemorrhage without intraventricular extension. At presentation his blood pressure was 190/100 mmHg and INR 3.2 while taking warfarin and aspirin, making hypertension and anticoagulation important contributors to the acute bleeding risk; no subsequent treatment or outcome is documented. He had a prior acute ischemic-stroke presentation in 2022 with NIHSS 12 and an initially negative CT, followed by another left-sided neurologic event in 2023 treated with alteplase and complicated by increasing confusion and worsening weakness; the result of the repeat CT is unavailable. Atrial fibrillation was confirmed in 2020 and has caused recurrent symptomatic episodes, complicating the balance between embolic prevention and intracranial bleeding risk. Biopsy in 2020 confirmed moderately differentiated ascending-colon adenocarcinoma with suspicious hepatic lesions and bilateral pulmonary nodules; current cancer treatment and disease status are not documented. He also had appendicitis in 2021 and subsequently underwent open appendectomy. Chronic therapies listed include metformin, lisinopril, hydrochlorothiazide, atorvastatin, aspirin, warfarin, and sustained-release morphine; renal function was preserved at the latest encounter (creatinine 1.0 mg/dL).

This approximately 40-year-old woman has recurrent pulmonary embolic disease: CT angiography confirmed a right segmental PE in January 2020, she had a similar suspected recurrence in July 2020, and she was hospitalized in January 2021 with another episode of abrupt dyspnea and pleuritic chest tightness and a right lower-lobe perfusion defect on CT pulmonary angiography. During the latest episode she was tachycardic (116/min), tachypneic (30/min), and hypoxemic (91% on room air), with respiratory alkalosis, sinus tachycardia, and a clear chest radiograph; blood pressure was preserved at 108/72 mmHg. Her ongoing thrombotic risk factors include estrogen-containing oral contraception, active smoking, prolonged sitting and repeated long-haul flights, with a family history of DVT in her mother and PE in a paternal uncle. Despite her prior PE, the only home medication documented is a combined oral contraceptive, with no anticoagulant listed; treatment and follow-up after the current presentation are not documented. Other active problems are migraine disorder, mild major depressive disorder, menstrual irregularity, and tobacco use disorder. Overall, the record shows repeated acute PE-like presentations over one year, culminating in the latest imaging-supported event without a documented resolution.

This man has hypertension, type 2 diabetes, stage 3a chronic kidney disease, coronary artery disease with prior drug-eluting stent, left hip osteoarthritis, and remote peptic ulcer disease; the chart lists him as 68, although encounter notes report older ages. Mild cognitive impairment diagnosed in 2020 progressed from memory complaints (MMSE 28/30) to impaired navigation, two minor driving accidents, and MMSE 24/30 by 2021; he takes donepezil. In 2023, weight loss and painless obstructive jaundice led to identification of a pancreatic head mass, subsequently documented as mucin-producing pancreatic adenocarcinoma with chronic disseminated intravascular coagulation; a biliary stent is recorded. He developed hypertensive flash pulmonary edema with hypoxemia in January 2024 and an episode of anterior ST-elevation chest pain with elevated CK-MB in July 2024, documented as myocardial reperfusion injury. In January 2025, gram-negative bacteremia caused distributive septic shock with lactic acidosis, worsening renal function, oliguria, encephalopathy, and hypoperfusion-related liver injury; abdominal CT raised concern for bowel ischemia and bacterial translocation. Most recently, in January 2026, abrupt left visual inattention, neglect of the left arm, and left-sided weakness with fluent speech and a nonhemorrhagic head CT are concerning for an acute right hemispheric ischemic stroke; definitive vascular imaging and outcome are not documented. His vascular risk factors and malignancy-associated coagulopathy complicate the current neurologic presentation, and the record does not establish the current cancer treatment status or recovery from prior shock.

This young adult man has a history of exertional rhabdomyolysis in January 2020 and cholera after travel to Mexico in July 2020; the latest documented encounter is an ED visit in July 2021 for a second episode of suspected cholera. After disaster-relief work in flood-affected rural Bangladesh with untreated-water and street-food exposure, he developed more than 15 episodes of profuse, nonbloody, rice-water diarrhea without fever or abdominal pain. Orthostatic lightheadedness, minimal urine output, hypotension, tachycardia, dry mucous membranes, and skin tenting indicate severe volume depletion with risk of prerenal acute kidney injury and electrolyte disturbances; no confirmatory testing or treatment outcome is documented for this episode. His prior Mexico-associated illness similarly caused high-volume noninflammatory watery diarrhea, mild dehydration, hypokalemia (3.1 mEq/L), hyponatremia (133 mEq/L), low bicarbonate (18 mEq/L), and creatinine of 1.3 mg/dL. The earlier exertional rhabdomyolysis followed a hot-weather endurance race and required fluid resuscitation; oliguria, elevated creatinine and potassium, and heme-positive urine without red cells were consistent with myoglobinuria and associated kidney injury. Thus, the documented trajectory is repeated acute dehydration-related illness rather than an established chronic renal disorder, and recovery or current renal function is not recorded. He is a never-smoker, drinks alcohol infrequently, has no recorded ongoing medications, and has no known drug allergies.

This woman has Hashimoto thyroiditis with hypothyroidism, celiac disease, primary adrenal insufficiency, a prolactinoma, left breast invasive ductal carcinoma, and restless legs syndrome. Her hypothyroidism has previously caused fatigue, proximal weakness, and elevated CK, particularly after she ran out of levothyroxine in 2022 (TSH 45, free T4 0.5); she is again taking levothyroxine, with TSH normalized to 2.5 in January 2024. Primary adrenal insufficiency presented in 2021 with weight loss, hyperpigmentation, orthostatic hypotension, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and hypoglycemia; she is maintained on hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone. Celiac disease was identified after diarrhea, weight loss, positive tissue-transglutaminase IgA, and iron-deficiency anemia; although her CBC normalized by 2023, ferritin remained low at 15, and she takes oral iron and vitamin D. Her prolactinoma, associated with hyperprolactinemia, irregular menses, and difficulty conceiving, is status post transsphenoidal macroadenoma resection and is treated with cabergoline. Left breast invasive ductal carcinoma was added to the problem list in 2023; she is status post lumpectomy and sentinel-node biopsy and takes tamoxifen, but staging and current surveillance findings are not documented. Restless legs symptoms disrupted sleep in 2023 in the setting of low iron stores. Most recently, she reports six months of burning and numb third-to-fourth toe interspace pain exacerbated by tight shoes or prolonged walking, with focal tenderness and a compression click, consistent with a symptomatic Morton neuroma; vital signs were normal, and no systemic deterioration was documented.
